idiom_name: UIApplicationDelegate: UIKit creates and calls your delegate
implementation_notes: UIKit owns the process: UIApplicationMain creates your app delegate and calls its methods at launch, activation, backgrounding and termination, so application code is a set of reactions to the system's schedule. The classic framework-hook structure survives verbatim as a protocol conformance (or as overrides of UIViewController lifecycle methods), which is the right form when the component must integrate with platform lifecycle events. The declarative SwiftUI form replaces the delegate with a value the system renders and re-evaluates.
pitfalls: Delegate callbacks arrive on the main thread and must return quickly; synchronous work in launch or activation callbacks delays the app and can trip the watchdog.
The system may terminate the process after background callbacks, so state that must survive belongs in persistent storage, not in delegate fields.

variants.name: Declarative app structure (SwiftUI App/View body)
variants.idiom_name: SwiftUI App/View: the framework runs the app value and re-evaluates body
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftUI pushes inversion further: the @main App type provides a default main() the system calls, and the framework evaluates your body property whenever state changes and renders the resulting scene graph, so you never issue drawing or scheduling calls yourself. The hook base class disappears entirely - extension is a value the framework reads - which is the modern default for UI code. Reach for the delegate/callback form when you need imperative control over lifecycle or platform APIs without a SwiftUI equivalent.
pitfalls: body must stay a pure description: side effects or expensive work there run on every re-evaluation, and SwiftUI decides how often that happens.
State ownership is part of the contract: plain stored properties are recreated when the framework re-creates the view, so persistent state needs @State/@StateObject and correct identity.
